newsitem.title: UK: Unshackled BoE won't send rates soaring - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Unshackled BoE won't send rates soaring - analysts.

text.p: The quarter-point rise in British interest rates announced on Tuesday is not the first step in a significant tightening of monetary policy, even if the Bank of England is now to a large degree independent, economists said.
"Where rates go from here is not much higher," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi International.

Britain's new Chancellor of the Exchequer, Gordon Brown, sanctioned the rise in base rates to 6.25 percent and at the same time announced sweeping changes to the monetary structure, giving the central bank more independence and removing the Treasury's say over setting interest rates.

"You could argue an independent Bank of England will push rates higher than the government would have done," Shepperd said. "But George has backed down in recent months and has only been demanding a quarter-point tightening, which is what he has got."
Bank of England Governor Eddie George has consistently called for higher interest rates this year.
But having hinted at the need for a half-point increase earlier in the year, he has recently tempered his demands.

Shepperd said although the government will retain control of setting the inflation target and reserves the right to override the Bank in "exceptional circumstances", the Bank is essentially now independent.
"Realistically you would expect the override to be used very rarely, if at all. In reality, what you have is an independent Bank of England," he said.
The Confederation of British Industry was quick off the blocks, saying any further policy tightening should come on the fiscal, not monetary side.
Sudhir Junankar, the CBI's associate director of economic analysis, told reporters Tuesday's rate rise would not curb bubbling domestic demand.
But he said Brown faced a policy dilemma, since the stellar, near 19 percent rise in sterling since last August was depressing exports leaving companies relying on domestic demand.
"The balance of policy tightening should fall on the fiscal side rather than on interest rates," he said. "The Chancellor will have the chance to address that in the mini-budget."

Brown has said he will hold a budget within two months of taking power. He has pledged to introduce a windfall tax on the privatised utilities and cut VAT on heating fuel. But some economists expect him to do much more.

Shepperd was not so sure. He said falling public sector debt -- it totalled about 23 billion stg in 1996/97, well below the government's 26.4 billion forecast -- and the tightening effect that the strong pound exerts, meant hefty tax rises were not on the cards.
"Brown has already proved himself to be a bold Chancellor so he could do anything, but we think only modest fiscal tightening is called for," he said.
Shepperd said base rates may be ratcheted up another notch to 6.5 percent but that should be enough.
Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS, said Brown could easily avoid base rates heading much higher by looking to the fiscal side of the equation.
"If Brown moves more towards fiscal policy to slow down growth, then the Bank of England will eventually see a less marked need for interest rate rises.
The short sterling strip was discounting rates at around 6.75 percent by the end of the year.
Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc, forecast Brown's budget would contain tax rises above and beyond the windfall tax.

He suggested exemption allowances on income tax levels could be restricted further and national insurance bands could be tinkered with. Others suggested the abolition of tax relief on home loan payments.

"The abolition of MIRAS would certainly be desirable and directed specifically at one point of the economy which really is growing fast," Shaw said. But he expected it to be phased out, not axed in one go.
Britain's housing market has recovered strongly in recent months with London and the South East seeing year-on-year price rises up to 20 percent.

But the Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors warned against choking off the housing recovery too violently. "Further (rate) rises, if coupled with the abolition of MIRAS, would leave thousands of homeowners worse off and widen the north/south divide," it said.
